segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: James, a slave of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes in the Diaspora: greetings.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Consider it nothing but joy, my brothers and sisters, whenever you fall into trials of many kinds,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: knowing that the testing of your faith produces endurance.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And let endurance have its perfect work, so that you may be perfect and whole, lacking in nothing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives to all without reservation and without reproach, and it will be given to him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But let him ask in faith, doubting nothing, for the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea, driven and tossed by the wind.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For that person must not suppose that he will receive anything from the Lord,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let the lowly brother boast in his high standing,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and the rich one in his being brought low, because like a flower of the grass he will pass away.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the sun rises with its scorching heat and dries up the grass, and its flower falls, and the beauty of its appearance is lost. So too the rich one will fade away in the midst of his pursuits.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Blessed is the man who endures trial, because once he has stood the test he will receive the crown of life, which God has promised to those who love him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: No one who is being tempted should say,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I am being tempted by God.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For God cannot be tempted by evil, and he himself tempts no one.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But each person is tempted by his own desire, dragged away and lured by it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then desire, once it has conceived, bears sin, and sin, once it is full-grown, gives birth to death.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do not be deceived, my beloved brothers and sisters.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: All good giving and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow cast by turning.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Of his own will he gave birth to us by the word of truth, so that we would be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Know this, my beloved brothers and sisters. Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for a man’s anger does not bring about the righteousness of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore, putting away all filthiness and the overflow of wickedness, receive with gentleness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But be doers of the word and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man who looks in a mirror at the face he was born with;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for he looks at himself and goes away, and at once forgets what he was like.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the one who peers into the perfect law, the law of freedom, and stays with it, becoming not a hearer who forgets but a doer who acts, that one will be blessed in his doing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If anyone thinks he is religious while not bridling his tongue but deceiving his own heart, that person’s religion is worthless.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to look after orphans and widows in their distress, and to keep oneself unstained by the world.

notes.note: The Greek name is Iakobos, the Greek form of the Hebrew name Jacob. 'James' is how English has come to spell it for New Testament figures. A first-century reader would have heard a man named Jacob addressing 'the twelve tribes', the descendants of the patriarch Jacob.

The Greek word ordinarily means a slave, someone owned by a master, and not a hired servant. Most English versions soften it to 'servant' or 'bondservant'. In the Greek Old Testament 'slave of the Lord' is also a title of honour for figures such as Moses, David and the prophets, so the word conveys both total belonging and dignity.

The term was the standard Jewish word for Jews living scattered outside the land of Israel. Whether the letter addresses Jewish followers of Jesus literally living abroad, or uses the phrase as a picture of the whole church as God's scattered people, is disputed.

The Greek plural, literally 'brothers', was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women as fellow members of a family or community. Many recent translations render it 'brothers and sisters' for that reason; older ones have 'brethren' or 'brothers'.

The same Greek word-family covers both an external trial that tests a person and an inner temptation to do wrong. It is rendered 'trial' in verses 2 and 12, where hardship to be endured is in view, and 'tempt' in verses 13–14, where enticement to evil is in view. English cannot keep the single word that links these passages in the Greek, and some interpreters read 'testing' throughout.

The Greek word means complete, having reached its goal, fully grown; it does not by itself mean flawless or sinless. Many modern versions have 'mature' for persons here. 'Perfect' is kept so that the repetition in this verse and the links to the 'perfect gift' (verse 17) and 'perfect law' (verse 25) stay visible.

The adverb basically means 'simply, with singleness of purpose', and so 'without holding back'. Most translations have 'generously', which is a possible extension of that sense. The rendering here keeps the contrast with the 'double-minded' person of verse 8: God gives with an undivided mind.

The Greek does not repeat 'brother', so it is unclear whether the rich person is a fellow believer told to take pride in being humbled, or an outsider whose only 'boast' is, ironically, his coming downfall. Both readings have scholarly support. The translation leaves the question as open as the Greek does.

The earliest manuscripts have no expressed subject: 'which he has promised'. Later manuscripts supply 'the Lord' or 'God'. 'God' is supplied here only because English 'he' would wrongly seem to refer to the person who endures.

The verb is the ordinary word for a mother giving birth. It is the same verb used in verse 15 of sin giving birth to death, and the contrast is deliberate. Older versions used the father's verb 'begat' or the neutral 'brought forth'; several modern versions have 'gave us birth'.

The Greek form can be either a command ('Know this') or a statement ('You know this'). Some later manuscripts read 'Therefore' instead, which lies behind the King James Version's 'Wherefore'. It is also unclear whether the phrase points back to verses 17–18 or forward to what follows.

The traditional 'meekness' now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not. It describes a humble, unassertive disposition, here the opposite of the anger of verses 19–20. 'Gentleness' or 'humility' is the usual rendering in modern translations.

The Greek word refers to the outward practice of worship (rites, observances and acts of devotion), not to a system of beliefs, which is what 'religion' often means today. The point is that the true observance God accepts is control of the tongue, care for the vulnerable and a clean life.

candidates.reason: Occurs throughout the New Testament both literally and as a self-designation of apostles, and translations vary between 'slave', 'servant' and 'bondservant'.
The noun and its verb πειράζω cover both 'trial/test' and 'temptation/tempt' across the Gospels, Paul, Hebrews and James, and the split needs one policy (including for the Lord's Prayer).
Recurs in Matthew, Paul, Hebrews and James, where 'perfect', 'mature' and 'complete' are all in use and inconsistent choices hide links between passages.
The plural address to mixed congregations occurs in nearly every letter and needs one decision between 'brothers' and 'brothers and sisters', plus a rule for the singular.
Ranges over 'life', 'self' and 'soul' across the New Testament, and 'soul' can import a later body–soul dualism the Greek does not always carry.
